newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Samsung Electronics sees sales up eight percent.
newsitem.headline: Samsung Electronics sees sales up eight percent.

text.p: Samsung Electronics Co Ltd, the world's leading maker of 16-megabit DRAM chips, said on Monday it planned to jack up sales by 8.1 percent this year by scaling back DRAM chip output while boosting that of other products.
Samsung said international prices of 16-megabit DRAMs, or dynamic random access memory chips, have fallen below production costs and would continue to undermine sales of the company's main product.
Company officials said semiconductor sales would fall to less than 30 percent of Samsung's total sales this year, from about 35 percent in 1996 and 40 percent in 1995.
Samsung Electronics, the flagship company of South Korea's Samsung Group, said it set a sales target for this year of 17.3 trillion won ($20 billion), up from 16 trillion won in 1996.
"Focus will be placed on future-oriented businesses, such as multimedia, display units and telecommunications manufacturing," Samsung spokesman Chung Deuk-si said.
"More than 80 percent of this year's investment, estimated at 4.5 trillion won, will be spent on those areas."
Samsung said sales of multimedia, telecommunications and information products would account for more than 30 percent of total sales this year, against about 23 percent in 1996.
Sales of consumer electronics would remain unchanged at about 35 percent.
Samsung, the world's largest manufacturer of 16-megabit DRAM chips, began reducing production of the chips in the fourth quarter of 1996 because of deteriorating profits.
Samsung said it plans to further cut production of memory chips until prices cover production costs.
"We may have to cut memory production by 20 to 30 percent this year. If the price does not rise to cover costs after that, a further reduction might be inevitable," Chung said.
Industry analysts said spot prices for 16-megabit DRAM chips now hovered at around $8, up from about $6 a month ago, but down sharply from about $40 to $50 a year ago.
"We believe the optimal price to cover costs would be around $10-$12," said Chung.

Samsung said it would use extra production capacity after cutting 16-megabit output to make other higher-value memory chips, such as graphic memory chips and non-memory chips. These would include application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs).
"As a result, non-memory chip production will rise to 15 percent of the total semiconductor production this year from 10 percent in 1996," Chung said.
Samsung said in a statement it set its overall domestic sales target at 7.5 trillion won for this year, against 6.1 trillion won last year.
The sales target excludes turnover of 3.4 trillion won to be generated by overseas subsidiaries and joint ventures this year. Such sales totalled 2.3 trillion won in 1996.
Its export target was set at 9.8 trillion won for 1997, compared with 1996 shipments of 9.9 trillion won.
"Exports will fall slightly as we expand overseas production. The need for direct sales is growing quite rapidly, especially when it comes to emerging markets," Chung said.
Production of consumer electronics would increase sharply in countries such as China, Malaysia and Brazil, he added.
